questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
In a qualitative analysis $\text{Bi}^{3+}$ is detected by appearance of precipitate of $\text{BiO(OH)(s)}$. Calculate pH when the following equilibrium exists at $298$ K :
$\text{BiO(OH)(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{BiO}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)}$,
$K = 4 \times 10^{-10}$
(Given : $\log 2 = 0.3010$)
questions.solution:
The equilibrium reaction is given by:

$\text{BiO(OH)(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{BiO}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)}$

The equilibrium constant expression is:

$K = [\text{BiO}^{+}][\text{OH}^{-}]$

Let the solubility of $\text{BiO(OH)}$ be $s$. Then $[\text{BiO}^{+}] = s$ and $[\text{OH}^{-}] = s$.

Substituting the values into the equilibrium expression:

$s^2 = 4 \times 10^{-10}$

$s = 2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ M}$

Therefore, the concentration of hydroxide ions is:

$[\text{OH}^{-}] = 2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ M}$

Calculating the pOH:

$\text{pOH} = -\log[\text{OH}^{-}] = -\log(2 \times 10^{-5}) = 5 - \log 2$

Given $\log 2 = 0.3010$:

$\text{pOH} = 5 - 0.3010 = 4.699$

The pH of the solution at $298 \text{ K}$ is:

$\text{pH} = 14 - \text{pOH} = 14 - 4.699 = 9.301$

Answer: $9.301$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At $298$ K, a certain buffer solution contains equal concentrations of $X^{-}$ and $HX$, $K_b$ for $X^{-}$ is $10^{-10}$. What is the pH of this buffer solution ?
questions.solution:
Given $K_b$ for $X^{-} = 10^{-10}$.

For a conjugate acid-base pair at $298$ K, $K_a \times K_b = K_w = 10^{-14}$.

$K_a = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-10}} = 10^{-4}$

The $pK_a$ of the weak acid $HX$ is:

$pK_a = -\log(K_a) = -\log(10^{-4}) = 4$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer:

$\text{pH} = pK_a + \log \left( \dfrac{[X^{-}]}{[HX]} \right)$

Since the concentrations of $X^{-}$ and $HX$ are equal, $[X^{-}] = [HX]$.

$\text{pH} = 4 + \log(1) = 4 + 0 = 4$

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The correct order of solubility of the given salts in water at $298$ K is
Salt$K_{sp}$ at 298 K
AgBr$5.0\times10^{-13}$
Zn(OH)_2$$1.0\times10^{-15}$
H$g_2$Cl_2$$1.3\times10^{-18}$
questions.solution:
Let $s$ be the solubility of the salt in water.

For $\text{AgBr}$:
$\text{AgBr} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ + \text{Br}^-$
$K_{sp} = s^2$
$s = \sqrt{5.0 \times 10^{-13}} = \sqrt{50 \times 10^{-14}} \approx 7.07 \times 10^{-7} \text{ M}$

For $\text{Zn(OH)}_2$:
$\text{Zn(OH)}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Zn}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$
$K_{sp} = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3$
$s = \left(\dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-15}}{4}\right)^{1/3} = \left(250 \times 10^{-18}\right)^{1/3} \approx 6.3 \times 10^{-6} \text{ M}$

For $\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$:
$\text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Hg}_2^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^-$
$K_{sp} = s(2s)^2 = 4s^3$
$s = \left(\dfrac{1.3 \times 10^{-18}}{4}\right)^{1/3} = \left(0.325 \times 10^{-18}\right)^{1/3} \approx 6.87 \times 10^{-7} \text{ M}$

Comparing the solubilities:
$6.3 \times 10^{-6} \gt 7.07 \times 10^{-7} \gt 6.87 \times 10^{-7}$

Thus, the correct order of solubility is $\text{Zn(OH)}_2 \gt \text{AgBr} \gt \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$.

Answer: $\text{Zn(OH)}_2\gt \text{AgBr}\gt \text{Hg}_2\text{Cl}_2$

questions.q:
Phosphoric acid ionizes in three steps with their ionization constant values $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_1}, \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}$ and $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3}$, respectively,
While K is the overall ionization constant.
Which of the following statements are true?
A. $\log \mathrm{K}=\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_1}+\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}+\log \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3}$
B. $\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4$ is a stronger acid than $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4^{-}$and $\mathrm{HPO}_4^{2-}$
C. $K_{a_1}\gt K_{a_2}\gt K_{a_3}$
D. $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_1}=\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_3}+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_2}}{2}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: For polybasic acid, order of ionization constant is $\mathrm{Ka}_1\gt\mathrm{Ka}_2\gt\mathrm{Ka}_3$ because as negative charge increases, tendency to loose $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions decreases. Overall $\mathrm{K}=\mathrm{Ka}_1 \times \mathrm{Ka}_2 \times \mathrm{Ka}_3$ Taking log on both sides $\log \mathrm{K}=\log \mathrm{Ka}_1+\log \mathrm{Ka}_2+\log \mathrm{Ka}_3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Phenolphthalein is used as an indicator for the titration of sodium hydroxide solution against a standard solution of oxalic acid. The colour change that is observed at an alkaline pH close to the equivalence point during this titration is :
questions.solution:
In the standardisation of sodium hydroxide using a standard solution of oxalic acid, oxalic acid (a primary standard) is taken in the conical flask and sodium hydroxide is taken in the burette.

Phenolphthalein is used as the indicator, which is colourless in an acidic medium and pink in an alkaline medium.

Initially, the solution in the conical flask contains oxalic acid, so it remains colourless.

As sodium hydroxide is added, the pH of the solution increases. At the equivalence point, the salt formed is sodium oxalate, which is a salt of a weak acid and a strong base. It undergoes anionic hydrolysis to give an alkaline solution.

At this alkaline pH (in the range of $8.2$ to $10.0$), the phenolphthalein indicator changes its colour to pink.

Thus, the observed colour change at the equivalence point is colourless to pink.

Answer: colourless to pink

questions.q: $\mathrm{pH}$ of a saturated solution of $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ is 12. The value of solubility product $K_{\text {sp }}$ of $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ is
questions.solution:
Given, $\mathrm{pH}$ of $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_2=12\begin{aligned}
\therefore \mathrm{pOH} & =14-\mathrm{pH} \\
& =14-12=2
\end{aligned}$
We know that,
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pOH} & =-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] \\
2 & =-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] \\
{\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] } & =\operatorname{antilog}(-2) \\
{\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] } & =1 \times 10^{-2}
\end{aligned}\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ dissolves in water as
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ba}_s^{2+}+2 \mathrm{OH}_2^{-} \\
& s \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \\
& \therefore \quad\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=2 s=1 \times 10^{-2} \\
& {\left[\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}\right] }=\frac{\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]}{2}=\frac{1 \times 10^{-2}}{2} \\
& K_{\text {sp }}=\left[\mathrm{Ba}^{2+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]^2
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& =\left(\frac{1 \times 10^{-2}}{2}\right)\left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2 \\
& =0.5 \times 10^{-6}=5 \times 10^{-7}
\end{aligned}$

A buffer solution is prepared in which the concentration of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is $0.30 \mathrm{M}$ and the concentration of $\mathrm{NH}_4^{+}$is $0.20 \mathrm{M}$. If the equilibrium constant, $K_b$ for $\mathrm{NH}_3$ equals $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$, what is the $\mathrm{pH}$ of this solution?
$(\log 2.7=0.43)$
questions.solution:
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pOH} & =\mathrm{p} K_{\mathrm{b}}+\log \frac{[\text { Salt }]}{[\text { Base }]} \\
& =-\log K_{\mathrm{b}}+\log \frac{[\text { Salt }]}{[\text { Base }]} \\
& =-\log 1.8 \times 10^{-5}+\log \frac{0.20}{0.30} \\
& =5-0.25+(-0.176) \\
& =4.75-0.176=4.57 \\
\therefore \mathrm{pH} & =14-4.57=9.43
\end{aligned}

Titration curve of NH4OH vs HClWB+SA

At the very beginning of the curve, the pH starts by falling quite quickly as the acid is added, but the curve very soon gets less steep. This is because a buffer solution is being set up composed of the excess ammonium hydroxide and the ammonium chloride being formed.

&
\end{aligned}$

both $(A)$ and $(R)$ are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COONa}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{NaOH}$
The above process takes place in following steps
$\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COONa} \underset{\text { in aqueous solution }}{\stackrel{\text { Ionisation }}{\rightleftharpoons}} \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOO}^{-}+\mathrm{Na}^{+}\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COO}^{-}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}$
Acetate ion undergoes anionic hydrolysis and the resulting solution is slightly basic due to excess of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ions. Hence, both (A) and (R) are true and $(R)$ is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
2. Given below are two statements
Statement I: The changes in $\mathrm{pH}$ with temperature are so small that we often ignore it
Statement II: When the hydrogen ion concentration changes by a factor of 100 , the $\mathrm{pH}$ changes by one unit In the light of above statements, identify the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both statements I and II are correct.
Both statements I and II are not correct.
Statement I is correct but statement II is not correct.
Statement I is not correct but statement II is correct.
questions.solution:
A small change in temperature has little impact on the $\mathrm{pH}$ of a solution as the concentration of the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions does not change much.
Thus, statement $\mathrm{I}$ is correct.
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{pH}_1=-\log \left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]_1 \text { so if }\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]_2=100\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]_1 \\
& \begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \mathrm{pH}_2 & =-\log \left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]_2=-\log \left(100\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]_1\right) \\
& =-\log (100)+\left[-\log \left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]_1\right] \\
& =-2+\mathrm{pH}_1=\mathrm{pH}_1-2
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}$
Thus, $\mathrm{pH}$ changes by two units.
Therefore, statement II is incorrect.

Identify the correct statements from the following.

(B) $\mathrm{pH}$ of a solution decreases with increasing temperature.
(C) $\mathrm{NaH}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4$ on hydrolysis gives a basic solution.
(D) $\mathrm{NH}_3$ can act both as Bronsted acid and base.
questions.solution:
(A) The ionic product of water at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is $51.3 \times 10^{-14}$. So, this statement is incorrect.
(B) On increasing the temperature, $\mathrm{pH}$ of solution also decreases.
(C) Since, $\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{HPO}_4$ is a salt of strong base $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and weak acid $\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4$, it gives a basic solution on hydrolysis.
(D). $\mathrm{NH}_3$ can act as both Bronsted acid and base because it can accept $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion to form $\mathrm{NH}_4^{+}$and donate $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion to form $\mathrm{NH}_2^{-}$.
Hence statements B, C, D are correct.

Kw increase with increase in temperature as dissociation of water increases with increase in temperature.

⇒pH=pKa+0 as salt=acid

questions.solution:
- (A) PbS: Lead sulfide is one of the least soluble metal sulfides. Therefore, it will have the lowest \(K_{s p}\) value from the list. The lowest value is \((1) 4.0 \times 10^{-53}\).
- (B) HgS: Mercury(II) sulfide is known to be one of the most insoluble compounds known. Its \(K_{s p}\) is exceptionally low. From the options, the value (II) \(8.0 \times 10^{-28}\) is the next lowest, which fits.
- (C) MnS: Manganese sulfide is a moderately soluble sulfide. Its \(K_{\text {sp }}\) is significantly higher than that of PbS or HgS, but still relatively low. This matches the third value, (IV) \(2.5 \times 10^{-13}\).
- (D) ZnS: Zinc sulfide is also a moderately soluble sulfide, often precipitated in basic solutions. Its \(K_{s p}\) is higher than that of MnS. The remaining value, (III) \(1.6 \times 10^{-24}\), is significantly higher than that of HgS and fits the profile for ZnS.
Therefore, the correct matches are A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III. This corresponds to option (2).

(2) (a) \(\rightarrow\) (p); (b) \(\rightarrow\) (r); (c) \(\rightarrow\) (q); (d) \(\rightarrow\) (s)
(3) (a) \(\rightarrow\) (r); (b) \(\rightarrow\) (s); (c) \(\rightarrow\) (p); (d) \(\rightarrow\) (q)

Here's the matched column:

\hline \text{(b)} & \mathrm{BaCrO}_4 & \text{(q)} & \mathrm{S}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}}{4}\right)^{1 / 3} \\
\hline \text{(c)} & \mathrm{Zr}_3\left(\mathrm{PO}_4\right)_4 & \text{(r)} & \mathrm{S}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}}{27}\right)^{1 / 4} \\
\hline \text{(d)} & \mathrm{Hg}_2 \mathrm{~L}_2 & \text{(s)} & \mathrm{S}=\left(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{s}}\right)^{1 / 2} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
Here's the matched column:
(a) \(\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{OH})_3(\mathrm{p}) 1 / 3 \mathrm{Ksp}[\mathrm{Al} 3+][\mathrm{OH}-] 3=\frac{1}{27}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{BaCrO}_4(\mathrm{q}) 1 / 2 \mathrm{Ksp}[\mathrm{Ba} 2+][\mathrm{CrO} 42-]=\frac{1}{4}\)

(d) \(\mathrm{Hg}_2 \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{~s}) \mathrm{Ksp}[\mathrm{Hg}^2_2+][\mathrm{I}-] 2=1\)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) values of four different silver salts at a certain temperature are given below:

Salt$K_{sp}$
$\text{AgCl}$$1.0 \times 10^{-10}$
$\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$$4.0 \times 10^{-12}$
$\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4$$2.7 \times 10^{-19}$
$\text{AgBr}$$1.0 \times 10^{-12}$


Which of the following salts has the highest molar solubility in water?
questions.solution:
To find the salt with the highest molar solubility, we calculate the molar solubility ($s$) for each salt from its $K_{sp}$.

1) For $\text{AgCl}$ (AB type):
$K_{sp} = s^2 \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 10^{-5}\text{ M}$

2) For $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ ($\text{A}_2\text{B}$ type):
$K_{sp} = 4s^3 \Rightarrow 4s^3 = 4.0 \times 10^{-12} \Rightarrow s^3 = 10^{-12} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

3) For $\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4$ ($\text{A}_3\text{B}$ type):
$K_{sp} = 27s^4 \Rightarrow 27s^4 = 2.7 \times 10^{-19} = 27 \times 10^{-20} \Rightarrow s^4 = 10^{-20} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-5}\text{ M}$

4) For $\text{AgBr}$ (AB type):
$K_{sp} = s^2 \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-12}} = 10^{-6}\text{ M}$

Comparing the values, $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ has the highest molar solubility ($10^{-4}\text{ M}$). A common mistake is to simply look for the highest $K_{sp}$ value (which is $\text{AgCl}$), but the stoichiometry of the salt must be considered when relating $K_{sp}$ to solubility.

Answer: $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The $\mathrm{pH}$ of a $0.05 \mathrm{~M}$ aqueous solution of a weak monoprotic acid is $3$. The acid dissociation constant $\left(K_{\mathrm{a}}\right)$ of this weak acid is :
questions.solution:
Given, concentration of the weak acid, $C = 0.05 \mathrm{~M}$

$\mathrm{pH} = 3$

We know that, $\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H}^+]$

$[\mathrm{H}^+] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}} = 10^{-3} \mathrm{~M}$

For a weak monoprotic acid, the acid dissociation constant $K_{\mathrm{a}}$ is approximated by:

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H}^+]^2}{C}$

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{0.05} = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{5 \times 10^{-2}}$

$K_{\mathrm{a}} = 0.2 \times 10^{-4} = 2 \times 10^{-5}$

Answer: $2 \times 10^{-5}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) of $Fe(OH)_3$ is $1.0 \times 10^{-36}$. The molar solubility of $Fe(OH)_3$ in a buffer solution maintained at $pH = 10$ is:
questions.solution:
In a buffer solution, the $pH$ is fixed, which means the $[OH^{-}]$ is also fixed and does not depend on the dissolution of the sparingly soluble salt.

Given $pH = 10$, we can find the $pOH$:
$pOH = 14 - 10 = 4$

Therefore, the hydroxide ion concentration is:
$[OH^{-}] = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

The dissociation of $Fe(OH)_3$ is:
$Fe(OH)_3 \rightleftharpoons Fe^{3+} + 3OH^{-}$

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{sp} = [Fe^{3+}][OH^{-}]^3$

Let the molar solubility of $Fe(OH)_3$ in this buffer be $s$. Then $[Fe^{3+}] = s$.
Substitute the fixed $[OH^{-}]$ into the expression:
$1.0 \times 10^{-36} = (s)(10^{-4})^3$
$1.0 \times 10^{-36} = s \times 10^{-12}$

Solving for $s$:
$s = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-36}}{10^{-12}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-24}\text{ M}$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{-24}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}$ is $1 \times 10^{-11}$. What is the molar solubility of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}$ in a buffer solution of $\mathrm{pH} = 12$?
questions.solution:
Given $\mathrm{pH} = 12$, the $\mathrm{pOH}$ of the buffer solution is $14 - 12 = 2$.

The concentration of hydroxide ions is $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}] = 10^{-2} \text{ M}$.

The dissociation of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}$ is given by:
$\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}(s)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Mg^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)}$

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{\mathrm{sp}} = [\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}][\mathrm{OH}^{-}]^{2}$

Let the molar solubility of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)_{2}}$ be $s$. Then $[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}] = s$. Since it is a buffer solution, $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ is fixed at $10^{-2} \text{ M}$.

Substituting the values:
$1 \times 10^{-11} = s \times (10^{-2})^{2}$
$10^{-11} = s \times 10^{-4}$
$s = 10^{-7} \text{ M}$

Option 1 is incorrect because it forgets to square the hydroxide ion concentration. Option 2 is incorrect because it uses the hydrogen ion concentration instead of the hydroxide ion concentration. Option 3 is incorrect because it calculates the solubility in pure water.

Answer: $10^{-7} \text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What volume of $0.2\text{ M}$ sodium benzoate solution must be added to $50\text{ mL}$ of $0.1\text{ M}$ benzoic acid to prepare a buffer solution of $\text{pH} = 4.5$?
[Given: $\text{pK}_\text{a}$ of benzoic acid $= 4.2$; $\log 2 = 0.3$]
questions.solution:
The mixture of benzoic acid and sodium benzoate forms an acidic buffer.

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation in terms of moles:
$\text{pH} = \text{pK}_\text{a} + \log \dfrac{n_{\text{salt}}}{n_{\text{acid}}}$

Given values:
$\text{pH} = 4.5$
$\text{pK}_\text{a} = 4.2$
Moles of acid ($n_{\text{acid}}$) $= M \times V = 0.1\text{ M} \times 50\text{ mL} = 5\text{ mmol}$

Substitute the values into the equation:
$4.5 = 4.2 + \log \left(\dfrac{n_{\text{salt}}}{5}\right)$
$0.3 = \log \left(\dfrac{n_{\text{salt}}}{5}\right)$

Since $\log 2 = 0.3$, we have:
$\dfrac{n_{\text{salt}}}{5} = 2$
$n_{\text{salt}} = 10\text{ mmol}$

The required volume of the $0.2\text{ M}$ sodium benzoate solution is:
$V_{\text{salt}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{salt}}}{M_{\text{salt}}} = \dfrac{10\text{ mmol}}{0.2\text{ M}} = 50\text{ mL}$

Answer: $50\text{ mL}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the solubility of $\text{PbSO}_4$ in a $0.05\text{ M}$ solution of $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$. (Given: $K_{\text{sp}}$ of $\text{PbSO}_4 = 1.5 \times 10^{-8}$)
questions.solution:
The strong electrolyte $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ dissociates completely in solution:
$\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}^{3+} + 3\text{SO}_4^{2-}$

The concentration of the common ion, $[\text{SO}_4^{2-}] = 3 \times 0.05\text{ M} = 0.15\text{ M}$.

For the sparingly soluble salt $\text{PbSO}_4$:
$\text{PbSO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq)$

Let the solubility of $\text{PbSO}_4$ in this solution be $s$.
The solubility product expression is:
$K_{\text{sp}} = [\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{2-}]$

Substituting the values (neglecting the small amount of $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ from $\text{PbSO}_4$):
$1.5 \times 10^{-8} = s \times (0.15)$

$s = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-8}}{0.15} = 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) of $Mg(OH)_2$ at $298\text{ K}$ is $3.2 \times 10^{-11}$. The $pH$ of its saturated aqueous solution at this temperature is:
(Given: $\log 2 = 0.3$)
questions.solution:
Let the molar solubility of $Mg(OH)_2$ be $s$.

The dissociation reaction is:
$Mg(OH)_2 \rightleftharpoons Mg^{2+} + 2OH^{-}$

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{sp} = [Mg^{2+}][OH^{-}]^2 = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3$

Given $K_{sp} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} = 32 \times 10^{-12}$

$4s^3 = 32 \times 10^{-12}$
$s^3 = 8 \times 10^{-12}$
$s = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

The concentration of hydroxide ions is:
$[OH^{-}] = 2s = 2 \times (2 \times 10^{-4}) = 4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

Now, calculate the $pOH$:
$pOH = -\log[OH^{-}] = -\log(4 \times 10^{-4})$
$pOH = 4 - \log 4 = 4 - 2\log 2$
$pOH = 4 - 2(0.3) = 4 - 0.6 = 3.4$

At $298\text{ K}$, $pH + pOH = 14$
$pH = 14 - 3.4 = 10.6$

Answer: $10.6$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Calculate the solubility of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ in a buffer solution of pH 12. Given that the solubility product ($K_{\text{sp}}$) of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is $1 \times 10^{-11}$.
questions.solution:
Given pH of the buffer solution = 12.

We know that $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14$
$\text{pOH} = 14 - 12 = 2$

Therefore, the concentration of hydroxide ions is:
$[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-\text{pOH}} = 10^{-2}\text{ M}$

The dissociation of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is given by:
$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq)$

Let the solubility of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ in the buffer be $s$. Then, $[\text{Mg}^{2+}] = s$.
Due to the buffer, the $[\text{OH}^-]$ is maintained at $10^{-2}\text{ M}$.

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{\text{sp}} = [\text{Mg}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$

Substitute the given values into the expression:
$1 \times 10^{-11} = s \times (10^{-2})^2$
$1 \times 10^{-11} = s \times 10^{-4}$

Solving for $s$:
$s = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-11}}{10^{-4}} = 1 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

Answer: $1 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In the titration of acetic acid against sodium hydroxide, what is the nature of the solution at the equivalence point, and what is the working pH range of the most suitable indicator for this titration?
questions.solution:
Acetic acid ($\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$) is a weak acid and sodium hydroxide ($\mathrm{NaOH}$) is a strong base. At the equivalence point, the salt formed is sodium acetate ($\mathrm{CH_3COONa}$).

Sodium acetate is a salt of a weak acid and a strong base. It undergoes anionic hydrolysis, making the solution basic at the equivalence point ($\mathrm{pH} \gt 7$).

The steep change in pH near the equivalence point for this titration lies in the basic region. Therefore, phenolphthalein is the most suitable indicator, which has a working pH range of approximately 8.0 to 9.8.

Answer: Basic, 8.0 - 9.8

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The pH of a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble metal hydroxide, $\text{M(OH)}_3$, at $298\text{ K}$ is $10.477$. What is the solubility product ($K_{\text{sp}}$) of $\text{M(OH)}_3$ at this temperature?
(Given: $\log 3 = 0.477$)
questions.solution:
First, find the pOH of the solution at $298\text{ K}$:
$\text{pOH} = 14 - \text{pH} = 14 - 10.477 = 3.523$

Using the given value $\log 3 = 0.477$, we can rewrite the pOH as:
$\text{pOH} = 4 - 0.477 = 4 - \log 3$

This corresponds to a hydroxide ion concentration of:
$[\text{OH}^{-}] = 3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

The dissociation of the metal hydroxide is:
$\text{M(OH)}_3\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^{3+}\text{(aq)} + 3\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)}$

If the solubility of $\text{M(OH)}_3$ is $s$, then $[\text{OH}^{-}] = 3s$.
$3s = 3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{\text{sp}} = [\text{M}^{3+}][\text{OH}^{-}]^3 = (s)(3s)^3 = 27s^4$

Substituting the value of $s$:
$K_{\text{sp}} = 27(10^{-4})^4 = 27 \times 10^{-16} = 2.7 \times 10^{-15}$

Answer: $2.7 \times 10^{-15}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A $0.05 \mathrm{~M}$ aqueous solution of a weak base is $2\%$ ionised. The $\mathrm{pH}$ of this solution is:
questions.solution:
For a weak base, the hydroxide ion concentration is given by:

$\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] = C \times \alpha$

Given concentration $C = 0.05 \mathrm{~M}$ and percentage ionisation $= 2\%$.
Degree of ionisation, $\alpha = \dfrac{2}{100} = 0.02$

$\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] = 0.05 \times 0.02 = 0.001 \mathrm{~M} = 10^{-3} \mathrm{~M}$

$\mathrm{pOH} = -\log\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] = -\log(10^{-3}) = 3$

Assuming standard temperature ($298 \mathrm{~K}$), $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14$
$\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 3 = 11$

The distractor $3$ is incorrect as it represents the $\mathrm{pOH}$, not the $\mathrm{pH}$. The distractors $1.3$ and $12.7$ result from incorrectly treating the weak base as a strong base.

Answer: $11$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List I with List II, where $s$ represents the molar solubility of the salt in water.

List I (Salt)List II ($K_{sp}$ expression)
(A) $\text{BaSO}_4$(I) $4s^3$
(B) $\text{CaF}_2$(II) $27s^4$
(C) $\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4$(III) $108s^5$
(D) $\text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3$(IV) $s^2$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For $\text{BaSO}_4$ (AB type):
$\text{BaSO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-}$
$K_{sp} = (s)(s) = s^2$

For $\text{CaF}_2$ (AB_2$ type): \\ $\text{CaF}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+} + 2\text{F}^-$ \\ $K_{sp} = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3$ \\ \\ For $\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4$ (A_3$B type):
$\text{Ag}_3\text{PO}_4 \rightleftharpoons 3\text{Ag}^+ + \text{PO}_4^{3-}$
$K_{sp} = (3s)^3(s) = 27s^4$

For $\text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3$ (A_2$B_3$ type):
$\text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Bi}^{3+} + 3\text{S}^{2-}$
$K_{sp} = (2s)^2(3s)^3 = (4s^2)(27s^3) = 108s^5$

Thus, the correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The ratio of the solubility of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ in pure water to its solubility in a $0.1\text{ M } \mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ solution is:
(Given : Solubility product of $\mathrm{BaSO_4} = 10^{-10}$)
questions.solution:
Let the solubility of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ in pure water be $s_1$.
For a 1:1 salt, $K_{sp} = s_1^2$
$s_1 = \sqrt{10^{-10}} = 10^{-5}\text{ M}$

Let the solubility of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ in $0.1\text{ M } \mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ be $s_2$.
Due to the common ion effect from $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$, the concentration of $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ is approximately $0.1\text{ M}$.
$K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}][\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}] = s_2 \times 0.1$
$10^{-10} = s_2 \times 10^{-1}$
$s_2 = 10^{-9}\text{ M}$

The required ratio is $\dfrac{s_1}{s_2} = \dfrac{10^{-5}}{10^{-9}} = 10^4$.

Answer: $10^{4}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
$100 \text{ mL}$ of $0.15 \text{ M}$ weak acid $\text{HA}$ is mixed with $100 \text{ mL}$ of $0.1 \text{ M}\text{NaOH}$. What is the $\text{pH}$ of the resulting solution?
[Given: $\text{pK}_\text{a}$ of $\text{HA} = 4.70$, $\log 2 = 0.30$, $\log 3 = 0.48$]
questions.solution:
Initial millimoles of $\text{HA} = 100 \times 0.15 = 15 \text{ mmol}$
Initial millimoles of $\text{NaOH} = 100 \times 0.1 = 10 \text{ mmol}$

The strong base $\text{NaOH}$ completely reacts with the weak acid $\text{HA}$ to form the salt $\text{NaA}$:
$\text{HA} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaA} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

Millimoles of $\text{NaA}$ formed $= 10 \text{ mmol}$
Millimoles of $\text{HA}$ remaining $= 15 - 10 = 5 \text{ mmol}$

The resulting solution is an acidic buffer. According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:
$\text{pH} = \text{pK}_\text{a} + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} \right)$

Since the volume is the same for both salt and acid in the mixture, we can use the ratio of their millimoles:
$\text{pH} = 4.70 + \log \left( \dfrac{10}{5} \right)$
$\text{pH} = 4.70 + \log 2$
$\text{pH} = 4.70 + 0.30 = 5.00$

Answer: $5.00$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Calculate the pH of a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble metal hydroxide, $\text{M(OH)}_2$, at $298\text{ K}$.
(Given: $K_{\text{sp}}$ of $\text{M(OH)}_2 = 3.2 \times 10^{-11}$, $\log 2 = 0.3$)
questions.solution:
The dissociation of the metal hydroxide is given by:
$\text{M(OH)}_2\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)}$

Let the solubility of $\text{M(OH)}_2$ be $s$.
Then, $[\text{M}^{2+}] = s$ and $[\text{OH}^{-}] = 2s$.

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{\text{sp}} = [\text{M}^{2+}][\text{OH}^{-}]^2 = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3$

Substituting the given $K_{\text{sp}}$:
$3.2 \times 10^{-11} = 4s^3$
$s^3 = 0.8 \times 10^{-11} = 8 \times 10^{-12}$
$s = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

The concentration of hydroxide ions is:
$[\text{OH}^{-}] = 2s = 2(2 \times 10^{-4}) = 4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

Calculating the pOH:
$\text{pOH} = -\log[\text{OH}^{-}] = -\log(4 \times 10^{-4}) = 4 - \log 4$
$\text{pOH} = 4 - 2\log 2 = 4 - 2(0.3) = 3.4$

The pH of the solution at $298\text{ K}$ is:
$\text{pH} = 14 - \text{pOH} = 14 - 3.4 = 10.6$

Answer: $10.6$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Determine the concentration of $\text{AgNO}_3$ required to reduce the solubility of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ to $1 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$. Given that the solubility product ($K_{\text{sp}}$) of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ is $4 \times 10^{-12}$.
questions.solution:
The target solubility of $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ is $s = 1 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$.

The dissociation of the sparingly soluble salt is:
$\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{CrO}_4^{2-}(aq)$

From the stoichiometry, the concentration of chromate ions is equal to the solubility:
$[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}] = s = 1 \times 10^{-8}\text{ M}$

Let the required concentration of $\text{AgNO}_3$ be $c$. Since $\text{AgNO}_3$ is a strong electrolyte, it completely dissociates to give $[\text{Ag}^+] \approx c$ (neglecting the very small amount of $\text{Ag}^+$ from $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$).

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{\text{sp}} = [\text{Ag}^+]^2[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]$

Substitute the known values into the expression:
$4 \times 10^{-12} = c^2 \times (1 \times 10^{-8})$

Solving for $c^2$:
$c^2 = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-12}}{1 \times 10^{-8}} = 4 \times 10^{-4}$

Taking the square root gives the required silver ion concentration:
$c = 2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ M}$

Thus, the required concentration of $\text{AgNO}_3$ is $2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ M}$.

Answer: $2 \times 10^{-2}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) of a sparingly soluble salt of the type $M_2X$ is $3.2 \times 10^{-11}$. What is the molar concentration of $M^+$ ions in its saturated aqueous solution?
questions.solution:
For a sparingly soluble salt of type $M_2X$, the dissociation equilibrium is:

$M_2X(s) \rightleftharpoons 2M^+(aq) + X^{2-}(aq)$

If the molar solubility of the salt is $s$, then at equilibrium:
$[M^+] = 2s$
$[X^{2-}] = s$

The solubility product $K_{sp}$ is given by:
$K_{sp} = [M^+]^2[X^{2-}] = (2s)^2(s) = 4s^3$

Given $K_{sp} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} = 32 \times 10^{-12}$:
$4s^3 = 32 \times 10^{-12}$
$s^3 = 8 \times 10^{-12}$
$s = (8 \times 10^{-12})^{1/3} = 2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$

The concentration of $M^+$ ions is:
$[M^+] = 2s = 2 \times (2 \times 10^{-4}) = 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$

Answer: $4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following mixtures will result in a buffer solution with maximum buffer capacity?
options: $30\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M HCOOH} + 30\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M KOH}$
$20\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M HCOOH} + 40\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M KOH}$
$40\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M HCOOH} + 20\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M KOH}$
$50\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M HCOOH} + 10\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M KOH}$
questions.solution:
A buffer solution has maximum buffer capacity when the concentration of the weak acid equals the concentration of its conjugate base (i.e., $\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a$). This requires neutralizing exactly half of the weak acid.

Let us calculate the millimoles (mmol) for the mixture in option 3:
Initial mmol of $\text{HCOOH} = 40\text{ mL} \times 0.2\text{ M} = 8\text{ mmol}$
Initial mmol of $\text{KOH} = 20\text{ mL} \times 0.2\text{ M} = 4\text{ mmol}$

The neutralization reaction is:
$\text{HCOOH} + \text{KOH} \rightarrow \text{HCOOK} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

Since $\text{KOH}$ is the limiting reagent, $4\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{KOH}$ will react with $4\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{HCOOH}$ to form $4\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{HCOOK}$.
Remaining $\text{HCOOH} = 8 - 4 = 4\text{ mmol}$.

The final solution contains $4\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{HCOOH}$ and $4\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{HCOOK}$. Since $[\text{Weak Acid}] = [\text{Salt}]$, the buffer has maximum capacity.

In contrast:
Option 1 forms only salt (complete neutralization).
Option 2 leaves excess strong base (not a buffer).
Option 4 leaves $8\text{ mmol}$ acid and $2\text{ mmol}$ salt (ratio $4:1$, not maximum capacity).

Answer: $40\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M HCOOH} + 20\text{ mL}$ of $0.2\text{ M KOH}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ ($K_{sp} = 3.2 \times 10^{-11}$) is more soluble in water than $\text{AgCl}$ ($K_{sp} = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}$).
Reason (R): For sparingly soluble salts, a higher numerical value of $K_{sp}$ always implies a higher molar solubility.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.
Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct.
questions.solution:
Let $s$ be the molar solubility.

For $\text{AgCl}$ (an AB type salt):
$K_{sp} = s^2$
$s = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ M}$

For $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ (an $\text{A}_2\text{B}$ type salt):
$K_{sp} = (2s)^2(s) = 4s^3$
$4s^3 = 3.2 \times 10^{-11} = 32 \times 10^{-12}$
$s^3 = 8.0 \times 10^{-12}$
$s = 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ M}$

Comparing the solubilities, $2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ M} \gt 1.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ M}$. Thus, $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$ is more soluble than $\text{AgCl}$, making the Assertion (A) correct.

The Reason (R) is incorrect because $K_{sp}$ values can only be directly compared to determine relative solubilities if the salts have the same stoichiometry. As shown here, $\text{AgCl}$ has a higher $K_{sp}$ ($10^{-10} \gt 10^{-11}$) but a lower molar solubility.

Answer: Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Equal volumes of $0.20\text{ M}$ ammonium hydroxide and $0.02\text{ M}$ ammonium chloride solutions are mixed together. What will be the $\text{pH}$ of the resulting solution?
[Given: $\text{pK}_\text{b}$ of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH} = 4.75$]
questions.solution:
The mixture of a weak base ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$) and its salt with a strong acid ($\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$) forms a basic buffer.

According to the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer:
$\text{pOH} = \text{pK}_\text{b} + \log \dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{base}]}$

Since equal volumes of the two solutions are mixed, the ratio of their concentrations in the mixture is equal to the ratio of their initial molarities.
$[\text{salt}] = 0.02\text{ M}$
$[\text{base}] = 0.20\text{ M}$

$\text{pOH} = 4.75 + \log \left(\dfrac{0.02}{0.20}\right)$
$\text{pOH} = 4.75 + \log (0.1)$
$\text{pOH} = 4.75 - 1 = 3.75$

The question asks for the $\text{pH}$ of the solution:
$\text{pH} = 14 - \text{pOH}$
$\text{pH} = 14 - 3.75 = 10.25$

Answer: $10.25$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $100$ mL of $0.2$ M weak acid $HA$ is mixed with $50$ mL of $0.2$ M $NaOH$ solution at $298$ K. If the base dissociation constant ($K_b$) for the conjugate base $A^{-}$ is $10^{-9}$, what is the pH of the resulting mixture?
questions.solution:
First, calculate the initial millimoles of the weak acid $HA$ and the strong base $NaOH$:

Millimoles of $HA = 100 \text{ mL} \times 0.2 \text{ M} = 20 \text{ mmol}$

Millimoles of $NaOH = 50 \text{ mL} \times 0.2 \text{ M} = 10 \text{ mmol}$

The neutralization reaction is:

$HA + NaOH \rightarrow NaA + H_2O$

Since $NaOH$ is the limiting reagent, $10 \text{ mmol}$ of $NaOH$ will react with $10 \text{ mmol}$ of $HA$ to form $10 \text{ mmol}$ of the salt $NaA$.

After the reaction, the mixture contains:

Remaining $HA = 20 - 10 = 10 \text{ mmol}$

Formed $A^{-} = 10 \text{ mmol}$

This forms an acidic buffer where the concentration of the weak acid equals the concentration of its conjugate base ($[HA] = [A^{-}]$).

Given $K_b$ for $A^{-} = 10^{-9}$.

For the conjugate acid-base pair, $K_a \times K_b = 10^{-14}$.

$K_a \text{ for } HA = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-9}} = 10^{-5}$

$pK_a = -\log(10^{-5}) = 5$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:

$pH = pK_a + \log \left( \dfrac{[A^{-}]}{[HA]} \right)$

$pH = 5 + \log(1) = 5 + 0 = 5$

Answer: $5$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The solution obtained by mixing $100\text{ mL}$ of $0.1\text{ M H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and $150\text{ mL}$ of $0.1\text{ M NaOH}$ is not a buffer.
Reason (R): The resulting solution contains an equimolar mixture of $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
Let us calculate the millimoles (mmol) of the acid and base mixed:
mmol of $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 = 100\text{ mL} \times 0.1\text{ M} = 10\text{ mmol}$
mmol of $\text{NaOH} = 150\text{ mL} \times 0.1\text{ M} = 15\text{ mmol}$

First equivalent of neutralization
$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
$10\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ reacts with $10\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ to form $10\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$.
Remaining $\text{NaOH} = 15 - 10 = 5\text{ mmol}$.

Second equivalent of neutralization
$\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$
The remaining $5\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{NaOH}$ reacts with $5\text{ mmol}$ of the newly formed $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$ to produce $5\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$.
Remaining $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4 = 10 - 5 = 5\text{ mmol}$.

The final solution contains $5\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$ (a weak acid) and $5\text{ mmol}$ of $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$ (its conjugate base).
Because it contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, the resulting mixture is indeed a buffer solution.

Therefore, the Assertion is false (it IS a buffer), but the Reason is true (it contains an equimolar mixture of $\text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{HPO}_4$).

Answer: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II.

Given: Solubility product ($K_{\mathrm{sp}}$) of $\mathrm{AgCl} = 10^{-10}$ and $K_{\mathrm{sp}}$ of $\mathrm{Ag_{2}CrO_{4}} = 4 \times 10^{-12}$.

List-IList-II (Molar solubility in M)
(A) $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in water(I) $10^{-9}$
(B) $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in $0.1 \text{ M KCl}$(II) $10^{-4}$
(C) $\mathrm{Ag_{2}CrO_{4}}$ in water(III) $4 \times 10^{-10}$
(D) $\mathrm{Ag_{2}CrO_{4}}$ in $0.1 \text{ M AgNO}_{3}$(IV) $10^{-5}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
(A) For $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in water: $K_{\mathrm{sp}} = s^{2} \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{10^{-10}} = 10^{-5} \text{ M}$. This matches (IV).

(B) For $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in $0.1 \text{ M KCl}$: $K_{\mathrm{sp}} = s \times [\mathrm{Cl}^{-}] \Rightarrow 10^{-10} = s \times 0.1 \Rightarrow s = 10^{-9} \text{ M}$. This matches (I).

(C) For $\mathrm{Ag_{2}CrO_{4}}$ in water: $K_{\mathrm{sp}} = 4s^{3} \Rightarrow 4 \times 10^{-12} = 4s^{3} \Rightarrow s^{3} = 10^{-12} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-4} \text{ M}$. This matches (II).

(D) For $\mathrm{Ag_{2}CrO_{4}}$ in $0.1 \text{ M AgNO}_{3}$: $K_{\mathrm{sp}} = [\mathrm{Ag}^{+}]^{2}[\mathrm{CrO_{4}^{2-}}] \Rightarrow 4 \times 10^{-12} = (0.1)^{2} \times s \Rightarrow s = 4 \times 10^{-10} \text{ M}$. This matches (III).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III).

Answer: (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A student needs to prepare an acidic buffer of $\text{pH} = 5.0$ using $0.1\text{ M CH}_3\text{COOH}$ ($\text{p}K_a = 4.7$) and $0.1\text{ M NaOH}$. What is the required volume ratio of $\text{NaOH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ to achieve this target pH? (Given $\log 2 = 0.3$)
questions.solution:
Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation:
$\text{pH} = \text{p}K_a + \log\left(\dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\right)$
$5.0 = 4.7 + \log\left(\dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\right)$
$\log\left(\dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\right) = 0.3$
Since $\log 2 = 0.3$, we have $\dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} = 2$

Let $V_b$ be the volume of $\text{NaOH}$ and $V_a$ be the volume of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.
Millimoles of $\text{NaOH} = 0.1 \times V_b$
Millimoles of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} = 0.1 \times V_a$

Upon mixing, the strong base completely reacts with the weak acid:
Millimoles of salt formed $= 0.1 \times V_b$
Millimoles of acid remaining $= 0.1 \times V_a - 0.1 \times V_b$

Substituting into the ratio:
$\dfrac{0.1 \times V_b}{0.1 \times V_a - 0.1 \times V_b} = 2$
$\dfrac{V_b}{V_a - V_b} = 2$
$V_b = 2V_a - 2V_b$
$3V_b = 2V_a$
$\dfrac{V_b}{V_a} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

The required volume ratio of $\text{NaOH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ is $2:3$.

Answer: $2:3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) of $\text{AgCl}$ is $1.6 \times 10^{-10}$. What is the molar solubility of $\text{AgCl}$ in a $0.1\text{ M}$ aqueous solution of $\text{NaCl}$?
questions.solution:
In a $0.1\text{ M}\text{NaCl}$ solution, the concentration of chloride ions is $[\text{Cl}^-] = 0.1\text{ M}$ (due to complete dissociation of $\text{NaCl}$).

Let the molar solubility of $\text{AgCl}$ in this solution be $s$.
The dissociation of $\text{AgCl}$ is:
$\text{AgCl}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$

At equilibrium:
$[\text{Ag}^+] = s$
$[\text{Cl}^-] = 0.1 + s \approx 0.1\text{ M}$ (since $s$ is very small compared to $0.1$)

The solubility product expression is:
$K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+][\text{Cl}^-]$
$1.6 \times 10^{-10} = (s)(0.1)$
$s = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-10}}{0.1} = 1.6 \times 10^{-9}\text{ mol/L}$

Thus, the molar solubility is $1.6 \times 10^{-9}\text{ mol/L}$.

Answer: $1.6 \times 10^{-9}\text{ mol/L}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II for buffer solutions at $298$ K containing equal concentrations of their respective conjugate acid-base pairs.

List-I (Buffer system and given constant)List-II (pH of the buffer)
(A) $HA / A^{-}$ with $K_b(A^{-}) = 10^{-9}$(I) $5$
(B) $BOH / B^{+}$ with $K_a(B^{+}) = 10^{-8}$(II) $6$
(C) $HX / X^{-}$ with $K_a(HX) = 10^{-6}$(III) $8$
(D) $YOH / Y^{+}$ with $K_b(YOH) = 10^{-5}$(IV) $9$


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For buffer solutions with equal concentrations of the conjugate acid-base pair, the logarithmic term in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation becomes zero ($\log 1 = 0$).

For acidic buffers: $\text{pH} = pK_a$
For basic buffers: $\text{pOH} = pK_b$ and $\text{pH} = 14 - \text{pOH}$

(A) Acidic buffer $HA / A^{-}$: Given $K_b(A^{-}) = 10^{-9}$.
$K_a(HA) = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-9}} = 10^{-5} \implies pK_a = 5$.
$\text{pH} = 5$. Matches (I).

(B) Basic buffer $BOH / B^{+}$: Given $K_a(B^{+}) = 10^{-8}$.
$K_b(BOH) = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-8}} = 10^{-6} \implies pK_b = 6$.
$\text{pOH} = 6 \implies \text{pH} = 14 - 6 = 8$. Matches (III).

(C) Acidic buffer $HX / X^{-}$: Given $K_a(HX) = 10^{-6}$.
$pK_a = 6 \implies \text{pH} = 6$. Matches (II).

(D) Basic buffer $YOH / Y^{+}$: Given $K_b(YOH) = 10^{-5}$.
$pK_b = 5 \implies \text{pOH} = 5$.
$\text{pH} = 14 - 5 = 9$. Matches (IV).

Correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Phenolphthalein is not a suitable indicator for the titration of aqueous ammonia against hydrochloric acid.

Reason (R): The pH at the equivalence point of this titration is less than 7, and the sharp change in pH does not overlap with the working range of phenolphthalein.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Aqueous ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$) is a weak base and hydrochloric acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$) is a strong acid. Their titration results in the formation of the salt $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$, which undergoes cationic hydrolysis, making the solution acidic at the equivalence point (pH < 7).

The sharp change in pH near the equivalence point for a strong acid-weak base titration occurs roughly between pH 7 and 3. Phenolphthalein has a working pH range of 8.0 to 9.8, which does not overlap with this sharp change. Therefore, phenolphthalein fails to indicate the end point accurately, making both the Assertion and the Reason true, with the Reason correctly explaining the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The $\mathrm{pH}$ of a $0.2 \mathrm{~M}$ aqueous solution of a weak monoprotic acid is $3$. What is the percentage ionisation of this acid?
questions.solution:
For a weak monoprotic acid, the hydrogen ion concentration is related to the $\mathrm{pH}$ by:

$\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}}$

Given $\mathrm{pH} = 3$, we have $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right] = 10^{-3} \mathrm{~M}$.

The relationship between $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]$, concentration $C$, and degree of ionisation $\alpha$ is:
$\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right] = C \times \alpha$

Given $C = 0.2 \mathrm{~M}$:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]}{C} = \dfrac{10^{-3}}{0.2} = 5 \times 10^{-3} = 0.005$

Percentage ionisation $= \alpha \times 100 = 0.005 \times 100 = 0.5\%$

The distractor $0.005\%$ is incorrect because it represents the fractional degree of ionisation without converting it to a percentage. The distractor $5\%$ is the result of a decimal place error.

Answer: $0.5\%$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At $298$ K, an acidic buffer solution containing a weak acid $HY$ and its salt $NaY$ has a pH of $5$. If the base dissociation constant ($K_b$) for the conjugate base $Y^{-}$ is $10^{-10}$, what is the ratio of the concentration of $Y^{-}$ to $HY$ in the buffer?
questions.solution:
Given $K_b$ for the conjugate base $Y^{-} = 10^{-10}$.

For a conjugate acid-base pair at $298$ K, $K_a \times K_b = K_w = 10^{-14}$.

$K_a = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-10}} = 10^{-4}$

The $pK_a$ of the weak acid $HY$ is:

$pK_a = -\log(K_a) = -\log(10^{-4}) = 4$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer:

$\text{pH} = pK_a + \log \left( \dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} \right)$

Substitute the given values ($\text{pH} = 5$):

$5 = 4 + \log \left( \dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} \right)$

$\log \left( \dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} \right) = 1$

Taking the antilogarithm on both sides:

$\dfrac{[Y^{-}]}{[HY]} = 10^1 = 10$

Thus, the ratio of the concentration of $Y^{-}$ to $HY$ is $10 : 1$.

Answer: $10 : 1$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Metal hydroxide and $K_{sp}$)List II ($[\text{OH}^-]$ in saturated solution)
(A) $\text{MOH}$, $K_{sp} = 10^{-10}$(I) $3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$
(B) $\text{M(OH)}_2$, $K_{sp} = 4 \times 10^{-12}$(II) $4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M}$
(C) $\text{M(OH)}_3$, $K_{sp} = 2.7 \times 10^{-15}$(III) $10^{-5}\text{ M}$
(D) $\text{M}'\text{(OH)}_2$, $K_{sp} = 3.2 \times 10^{-14}$(IV) $2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For $\text{MOH}$: $K_{sp} = s^2 = 10^{-10} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-5}\text{ M}$.
$[\text{OH}^-] = s = 10^{-5}\text{ M}$. (A matches III)

For $\text{M(OH)}_2$: $K_{sp} = 4s^3 = 4 \times 10^{-12} \Rightarrow s^3 = 10^{-12} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$.
$[\text{OH}^-] = 2s = 2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$. (B matches IV)

For $\text{M(OH)}_3$: $K_{sp} = 27s^4 = 2.7 \times 10^{-15} = 27 \times 10^{-16} \Rightarrow s^4 = 10^{-16} \Rightarrow s = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$.
$[\text{OH}^-] = 3s = 3 \times 10^{-4}\text{ M}$. (C matches I)

For $\text{M}'\text{(OH)}_2$: $K_{sp} = 4s^3 = 3.2 \times 10^{-14} = 32 \times 10^{-15} \Rightarrow s^3 = 8 \times 10^{-15} \Rightarrow s = 2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M}$.
$[\text{OH}^-] = 2s = 4 \times 10^{-5}\text{ M}$. (D matches II)

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At $298$ K, a basic buffer solution contains equal concentrations of a weak base $B$ and its conjugate acid $BH^{+}$. If the acid dissociation constant ($K_a$) for $BH^{+}$ is $10^{-9}$, what is the pH of this buffer solution?
questions.solution:
Given $K_a$ for the conjugate acid $BH^{+} = 10^{-9}$.

For a conjugate acid-base pair at $298$ K, $K_a \times K_b = K_w = 10^{-14}$.

The base dissociation constant ($K_b$) for the weak base $B$ is:

$K_b = \dfrac{10^{-14}}{10^{-9}} = 10^{-5}$

The $pK_b$ of the weak base is:

$pK_b = -\log(K_b) = -\log(10^{-5}) = 5$

Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for a basic buffer:

$pOH = pK_b + \log \left( \dfrac{[BH^{+}]}{[B]} \right)$

Since the concentrations of $B$ and $BH^{+}$ are equal, $[BH^{+}] = [B]$.

$pOH = 5 + \log(1) = 5 + 0 = 5$

The pH of the solution is calculated as:

$pH = 14 - pOH = 14 - 5 = 9$

Answer: $9$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List I with List II for the selection of a suitable indicator in different acid-base titrations.

List I (Titration)List II (Suitable Indicator)
(A) $\mathrm{HCl}$ vs $\mathrm{NaOH}$(I) Phenolphthalein
(B) $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ vs $\mathrm{NaOH}$(II) Methyl orange
(C) $\mathrm{HCl}$ vs $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$(III) Any of these
(D) $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ vs $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$(IV) None of these

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Titration of a strong acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$) and strong base ($\mathrm{NaOH}$) has a sharp pH change from about 3 to 11 at the equivalence point, so any of these indicators (phenolphthalein or methyl orange) can be used.

Titration of a weak acid ($\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$) and strong base ($\mathrm{NaOH}$) has an equivalence point in the basic region (pH > 7) due to anionic hydrolysis, making phenolphthalein (working range 8.0-9.8) suitable.

Titration of a strong acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$) and weak base ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$) has an equivalence point in the acidic region (pH < 7) due to cationic hydrolysis, making methyl orange (working range 3.1-4.4) suitable.

Titration of a weak acid ($\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$) and weak base ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$) does not produce a sharp change in pH at the equivalence point, so none of these simple indicators are suitable.

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product constant ($K_{sp}$) of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is $1.0 \times 10^{-11}$. The molar solubility of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ in a buffer solution of pH $12$ is:
questions.solution:
Given pH $= 12$, the pOH can be calculated as:
$\text{pOH} = 14 - \text{pH} = 14 - 12 = 2$
Therefore, the concentration of hydroxide ions is $[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-2}\text{ M}$.

Since the solution is buffered, the $[\text{OH}^-]$ remains fixed at $10^{-2}\text{ M}$.

The dissociation of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is:
$\text{Mg(OH)}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$

Let $s$ be the molar solubility of $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$. Then $[\text{Mg}^{2+}] = s$.

The expression for the solubility product is:
$K_{sp} = [\text{Mg}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$

Substituting the given values:
$1.0 \times 10^{-11} = (s)(10^{-2})^2$
$1.0 \times 10^{-11} = s \times 10^{-4}$
$s = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-11}}{10^{-4}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

The molar solubility is $1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$.

Answer: $1.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match the acid-base mixtures in List I with the nature of the resulting solution in List II.

(A)$100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M CH}_3\text{COOH} + 50\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M NaOH}$(I)Acidic buffer
(B)$100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M NH}_4\text{OH} + 100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M HCl}$(II)Basic salt solution
(C)$100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M HCl} + 100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M NaOH}$(III)Acidic salt solution
(D)$100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M CH}_3\text{COOH} + 100\text{ mL of } 0.1\text{ M NaOH}$(IV)Neutral solution

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Calculate the millimoles of acid and base for each mixture:

(A) $10\text{ mmol CH}_3\text{COOH} + 5\text{ mmol NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{ mmol CH}_3\text{COOH} + 5\text{ mmol CH}_3\text{COONa}$. This is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base, forming an acidic buffer (I).

(B) $10\text{ mmol NH}_4\text{OH} + 10\text{ mmol HCl} \rightarrow 10\text{ mmol NH}_4\text{Cl}$. Complete neutralization forms the salt of a weak base and strong acid, which undergoes cationic hydrolysis to give an acidic salt solution (III).

(C) $10\text{ mmol HCl} + 10\text{ mmol NaOH} \rightarrow 10\text{ mmol NaCl}$. Complete neutralization forms the salt of a strong acid and strong base, which does not hydrolyze, resulting in a neutral solution (IV).

(D) $10\text{ mmol CH}_3\text{COOH} + 10\text{ mmol NaOH} \rightarrow 10\text{ mmol CH}_3\text{COONa}$. Complete neutralization forms the salt of a weak acid and strong base, which undergoes anionic hydrolysis to give a basic salt solution (II).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): According to Ostwald's dilution law, the degree of ionization of a weak electrolyte is inversely proportional to the square root of its concentration.

Reason (R): When a $0.1 \mathrm{~M}$ solution of a weak acid is diluted to $0.01 \mathrm{~M}$, its degree of ionization $(\alpha)$ increases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true because Ostwald's dilution law states that for a weak electrolyte, the degree of ionization $\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_{\mathrm{a}}}{C}}$, which means $\alpha \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{C}}$.

Reason (R) is also true because as concentration decreases from $0.1 \mathrm{~M}$ to $0.01 \mathrm{~M}$ (dilution), the degree of ionization increases.

However, Reason (R) is merely a specific observation or consequence of Ostwald's dilution law, not its explanation. The law itself is derived from the equilibrium constant expression. Therefore, both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A sparingly soluble salt of the type $XY_2$ has a molar solubility of $2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$ in its saturated aqueous solution. What is the solubility product ($K_{sp}$) of this salt?
questions.solution:
For a sparingly soluble salt of type $XY_2$, the dissociation equilibrium is:

$XY_2(s) \rightleftharpoons X^{2+}(aq) + 2Y^-(aq)$

If the molar solubility is $s$, then at equilibrium:
$[X^{2+}] = s$
$[Y^-] = 2s$

The solubility product $K_{sp}$ is given by:
$K_{sp} = [X^{2+}][Y^-]^2 = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3$

Given $s = 2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$:
$K_{sp} = 4 \times (2 \times 10^{-3})^3$
$K_{sp} = 4 \times (8 \times 10^{-9}) = 32 \times 10^{-9} = 3.2 \times 10^{-8}$

Answer: $3.2 \times 10^{-8}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two sparingly soluble salts, $\text{MX}$ and $\text{MX}_3$, have the same molar solubility $s$ in water at a given temperature. The ratio of their solubility products, $K_{sp}(\text{MX}) : K_{sp}(\text{MX}_3)$, is
questions.solution:
For the salt $\text{MX}$:
$\text{MX} \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^+ + \text{X}^-$
$K_{sp}(\text{MX}) = (s)(s) = s^2$

For the salt $\text{MX}_3$:
$\text{MX}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^{3+} + 3\text{X}^-$
$K_{sp}(\text{MX}_3) = (s)(3s)^3 = 27s^4$

The ratio of their solubility products is:
$\dfrac{K_{sp}(\text{MX})}{K_{sp}(\text{MX}_3)} = \dfrac{s^2}{27s^4} = \dfrac{1}{27s^2}$

Thus, the ratio is $1 : 27s^2$.

Answer: $1 : 27s^2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Arrange the solubility of $\text{AgCl}$ in the following four different solvents in decreasing order:
I. $0.1\text{ M AgNO}_3$
II. $0.1\text{ M NaCl}$
III. $0.1\text{ M BaCl}_2$
IV. Pure water
questions.solution:
The solubility of a sparingly soluble salt like $\text{AgCl}$ is inversely proportional to the concentration of the common ion due to the common ion effect.

In pure water (IV), there is no common ion effect, so the solubility is maximum.

In $0.1\text{ M AgNO}_3$ (I), the common ion is $\text{Ag}^+$ and its concentration is $0.1\text{ M}$.

In $0.1\text{ M NaCl}$ (II), the common ion is $\text{Cl}^-$ and its concentration is $0.1\text{ M}$.

In $0.1\text{ M BaCl}_2$ (III), the common ion is $\text{Cl}^-$. Since one mole of $\text{BaCl}_2$ provides two moles of $\text{Cl}^-$, the concentration is $[\text{Cl}^-] = 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2\text{ M}$.

Since the common ion concentration is highest in III, the solubility of $\text{AgCl}$ will be the lowest in III.

Since I and II have the same concentration of common ions ($0.1\text{ M}$), the solubility of $\text{AgCl}$ in both will be equal.

Thus, the decreasing order of solubility is IV > I = II > III.

Answer: IV > I = II > III

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An aqueous solution of ammonium hydroxide is taken in a conical flask and titrated against standard hydrochloric acid from a burette. Which of the following is the most suitable indicator for this titration and what is the colour change observed at the end point?
questions.solution:
Ammonium hydroxide ($\mathrm{NH_4OH}$) is a weak base and hydrochloric acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$) is a strong acid. The salt formed at the equivalence point is ammonium chloride ($\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$), which undergoes cationic hydrolysis to give an acidic solution ($\mathrm{pH} \lt 7$).

For a strong acid-weak base titration, methyl orange is the suitable indicator. Since the indicator is added to the weak base in the conical flask, its initial colour in the basic medium is yellow. At the end point, the addition of a slight excess of strong acid changes the medium to acidic, turning the indicator red.

Answer: Methyl orange, yellow to red

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The solubility of $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in an aqueous $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution is $10^{-3}$ times its solubility in pure water. What is the concentration of $\mathrm{NaCl}$ in the solution?
(Given : Solubility product of $\mathrm{AgCl} = 10^{-10}$)
questions.solution:
Let the solubility of $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in pure water be $s_0$.
$K_{sp} = s_0^2$
$s_0 = \sqrt{10^{-10}} = 10^{-5}\text{ M}$

The solubility of $\mathrm{AgCl}$ in the $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution ($s$) is given as $10^{-3}$ times its solubility in pure water.
$s = 10^{-3} \times s_0 = 10^{-3} \times 10^{-5} = 10^{-8}\text{ M}$

In the $\mathrm{NaCl}$ solution, the chloride ion concentration is mainly due to $\mathrm{NaCl}$ (common ion effect). Let the concentration of $\mathrm{NaCl}$ be $C$.
$K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ag^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}] = s \times C$
$10^{-10} = 10^{-8} \times C$
$C = \dfrac{10^{-10}}{10^{-8}} = 10^{-2}\text{ M}$

Answer: $10^{-2}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) of a sparingly soluble hydroxide $\text{X(OH)}_2$ is $4 \times 10^{-15}$ at $298\text{ K}$. What is the solubility of $\text{X(OH)}_2$ in a buffer solution maintained at $\text{pH} = 10$?
questions.solution:
Given $\text{pH} = 10$, we have $\text{pOH} = 14 - 10 = 4$.

Thus, the hydroxide ion concentration is $[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-4}\text{ M}$.

For the sparingly soluble salt $\text{X(OH)}_2$, the dissociation equilibrium is:

$\text{X(OH)}_2\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{X}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$

The solubility product expression is:

$K_{sp} = [\text{X}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$

Let the solubility of $\text{X(OH)}_2$ in the buffer be $s$. Then $[\text{X}^{2+}] = s$.

Since the solution is buffered at $\text{pH} = 10$, the $[\text{OH}^-]$ is fixed at $10^{-4}\text{ M}$.

Substituting the values into the $K_{sp}$ expression:

$4 \times 10^{-15} = s(10^{-4})^2$

$4 \times 10^{-15} = s \times 10^{-8}$

$s = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-15}}{10^{-8}} = 4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

The solubility of $\text{X(OH)}_2$ is $4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$.

Answer: $4 \times 10^{-7}\text{ M}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II for the $\text{pH}$ of various equal-volume mixtures.
[Given: $\text{pK}_\text{a}$ of weak acid $\text{HA} = 4.0$, $\text{pK}_\text{b}$ of weak base $\text{BOH} = 5.0$ at $298 \text{ K}$]

List-I (Mixture)List-II (pH)
(A) $0.1 \text{ M HA} + 0.1 \text{ M NaA}$(I) $3.0$
(B) $0.1 \text{ M HA} + 1.0 \text{ M NaA}$(II) $4.0$
(C) $1.0 \text{ M HA} + 0.1 \text{ M NaA}$(III) $5.0$
(D) $0.1 \text{ M BOH} + 0.1 \text{ M BCl}$(IV) $9.0$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
For acidic buffers, $\text{pH} = \text{pK}_\text{a} + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} \right)$

(A) $[\text{Salt}] = [\text{Acid}] = 0.1 \text{ M}$.
$\text{pH} = 4.0 + \log(1) = 4.0$

(B) $[\text{Salt}] = 1.0 \text{ M}$, $[\text{Acid}] = 0.1 \text{ M}$.
$\text{pH} = 4.0 + \log\left(\dfrac{1.0}{0.1}\right) = 4.0 + \log(10) = 5.0$

(C) $[\text{Salt}] = 0.1 \text{ M}$, $[\text{Acid}] = 1.0 \text{ M}$.
$\text{pH} = 4.0 + \log\left(\dfrac{0.1}{1.0}\right) = 4.0 - 1 = 3.0$

For basic buffers, $\text{pOH} = \text{pK}_\text{b} + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]} \right)$

(D) $[\text{Salt}] = [\text{Base}] = 0.1 \text{ M}$.
$\text{pOH} = 5.0 + \log(1) = 5.0$
$\text{pH} = 14 - \text{pOH} = 14 - 5.0 = 9.0$

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If the pH of a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt $\text{M(OH)}_2$ is increased from $8$ to $9$, its solubility decreases by a factor of $100$.

Reason (R): For a sparingly soluble salt of type $\text{M(OH)}_2$, the solubility ($s$) is inversely proportional to the hydroxide ion concentration ($[\text{OH}^-]$).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
The dissociation of $\text{M(OH)}_2$ is given by:

$\text{M(OH)}_2\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$

The solubility product is $K_{sp} = [\text{M}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$.

If the solubility is $s$, then $[\text{M}^{2+}] = s$. Therefore, $s = \dfrac{K_{sp}}{[\text{OH}^-]^2}$.

This shows that solubility $s$ is inversely proportional to the square of the hydroxide ion concentration ($[\text{OH}^-]^2$), not just $[\text{OH}^-]$. Thus, the Reason (R) is false.

When pH increases from $8$ to $9$, the pOH decreases from $6$ to $5$. This means $[\text{OH}^-]$ increases from $10^{-6}\text{ M}$ to $10^{-5}\text{ M}$, which is an increase by a factor of $10$.

Since $s \propto \dfrac{1}{[\text{OH}^-]^2}$, when $[\text{OH}^-]$ increases by a factor of $10$, the solubility $s$ becomes $\dfrac{1}{10^2} = \dfrac{1}{100}$ of its original value. Hence, the solubility decreases by a factor of $100$. Thus, the Assertion (A) is true.

Therefore, Assertion is true but Reason is false.

Answer: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The solubility of sparingly soluble $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ increases when the pH of the solution is decreased.
Reason (R): Addition of $\text{H}^+$ ions consumes $\text{OH}^-$ ions to form water, shifting the equilibrium $\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Al}^{3+}(aq) + 3\text{OH}^-(aq)$ in the forward direction.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is not correct.
Assertion (A) is not correct but Reason (R) is correct.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) states that the solubility of $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ increases when pH is decreased (i.e., in an acidic medium). This is correct because $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ dissolves in acids.

Reason (R) explains this using Le Chatelier's principle. The dissolution equilibrium is $\text{Al(OH)}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Al}^{3+}(aq) + 3\text{OH}^-(aq)$. When pH is decreased, the added $\text{H}^+$ ions react with $\text{OH}^-$ ions to form unionised water. This decreases the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ in the solution. According to Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts in the forward direction to counteract this change, thereby increasing the solubility of $\text{Al(OH)}_3$.

Thus, both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.solution:
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{K}_{s p}= 3.2 \times 10^{-11} \\
& \mathrm{AX}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{X}^{-} \\
& \mathrm{S} \quad 2 \mathrm{~S} \\
& \mathrm{~K}_{s p}= \mathrm{S} \times(2 \mathrm{~S})^2=4 \mathrm{~S}^3 ; \\
&= 3.2 \times 10^{-11}=4 \mathrm{~S}^3
\end{aligned}

or, $\quad \mathrm{S}^3=0.8 \times 10^{-11}=8 \times 10^{-12}$
\therefore \quad \mathrm{S}=2 \times 10^{-4} \text {. }

Related Theory
The solubility of a substance in a solvent is the total amount of the solute that can be dissolved in the solvent at equilibrium. On the other hand, the solubility product constant is an equilibrium constant that provides insight into the equilibrium between the solid solute and its constituent ions that are dissociated across the solution.

questions.q: Which has highest $\mathrm{pH}$ ?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{NaNO}_3$ is salt formed by the combination of a strong acid $\mathrm{HNO}_3$ and a strong base $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and hence it is neutral with a $\mathrm{pH}$.
$\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOK}$ is formed by the combination of weak acid $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$ and strong base $\mathrm{KOH}$ and hence $\mathrm{pH}$ will be above 7 .
$\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{Cl}$ is formed by the formation of strong and $\mathrm{HCl}$ and a weak base $\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{OH}$ and hence $\mathrm{pH}$ will be lesser than 7.
$\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{CO}_3$ is a salt formed by the strong base $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and weak acid $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{CO}_3$. Hence, $\mathrm{pH}$ of the salt will be highest.
The pH scale was invented in 1909 by a Danish biochemist Soren Sorensen. It describes how many hydrogen ions (protons) are present in a solution: the higher the pH, the lower the hydrogen ion concentration, and vice versa. But the scale does not have fixed limits, so it is indeed possible to have a pH above 14 or below zero. For example, concentrated hydrochloric acid can have a pH of around -1 , while sodium hydroxide solution can have a pH as high as 15 .

questions.q: If the solubility of $\mathrm{MX}_2$ type electrolyte is $0.5 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$, then, find out $\mathrm{K}_{s p}$ of the electrolyte.
questions.solution:
An electrolyte \(\mathrm{MX}_2\) undergoes dissociation as follows :-
\(\mathrm{MX}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{M}^{+2}+2 \mathrm{X}^{-}\)
\(\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \text {Concentration } & \mathrm{MX}_2 & \mathrm{M}^{+2} & \mathrm{X}^{-} \\
\hline \text {Initial concentration } & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
\hline \text {Concentration at Equilibrium } & 1-\mathrm{s} & \mathrm{s} & 2 \mathrm{~s} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
Thus from the above condition we can say that,
\(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=\mathrm{s} \times(2 \mathrm{~s})^2=4 \times(\mathrm{s})^3\)
Here, s (the solubility) is \(0.5 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~mole} / \mathrm{lit}\).
\(\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=4 \times\left(0.5 \times 10^{-4}\right)^3 \\
& \therefore \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=5 \times 10^{-13}
\end{aligned}\)

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{N}_{\text {Mix }} \mathrm{V}_{\text {Mix }}=\underset{\text { (Base) }}{\mathrm{N}_1 \mathrm{~V}_1}-\underset{\text { (Acid) }}{\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{~V}_2}\ldots(i)$
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{M}_1 & =0.2 \mathrm{M}, \mathrm{N}_1=0.2 \mathrm{~N} \\
\mathrm{M}_2 & =0.1 \mathrm{M}, \mathrm{N}_2=0.1 \mathrm{~N} \\
\mathrm{~V}_1 & =50 \mathrm{ml}, \\
\mathrm{V}_2 & =50 \mathrm{ml}, \mathrm{V}_{\text {mix }}=100 \mathrm{ml}
\end{aligned}$
On substituting the given values is equation. (i), We get
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{N}_{\text {mix }} \times 100 & =50 \times 0.2-50 \times 0.1 \\
\mathrm{~N}_{\text {mix }} & =\frac{5}{100}=5 \times 10^{-2} \\
\therefore \quad\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] & =5 \times 10^{-2}
\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned}
{ }_{\mathrm{P}} \mathrm{OH} & =-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=-\log \left[5 \times 10^{-2}\right] \\
& =2-\log 5=1.3
\end{aligned}$
Also, $\mathrm{pH}+\mathrm{pOH}=14\mathrm{pH}=14-1.3=12.7$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Given pH of a solution $A$ is 3 and it is mixed with another solution $B$ having pH 2 . If both mixed, then resultant pH of the solution will be :
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{pH} \text { of } A=3 \quad \mathrm{pH} \text { of } B=2 \\ & \therefore\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=10^{-3} \mathrm{M}, \quad\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=10^{-2} \mathrm{M} \\ & \text { Total }\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right] \\ & =10^{-3}+10^{-2}=10^{-3}+10 \times 10^{-3} \\ & =11 \times 10^{-3} \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log \left(11 \times 10^{-3}\right) \\ & =3-\log 11 \\ & =3-1.04=1.96 \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The pH of a $10^{-10} \mathrm{M}-\mathrm{NaOH}$ solution is
questions.solution:
When the solution is very dilute, the concentration of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$produced from water cannot be neglected. Hence,
$\begin{aligned} & {\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=10^{-10}+10^{-7}} \\ & \text { (obtained from water) } \\ & =10^{-7}(0.001+1)=1.001 \times 10^{-7} \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{pOH}=-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] \\ & =-\log \left(1.001 \times 10^{-7}\right) \\ & =7-0.01=6.99 \\ & \therefore \quad \mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH} \\ & =14-6.99=7.01 \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which has minimum solubility?
questions.solution:
Solubilities of salts are as follows :
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Bi}_2 \mathrm{~S}_3 & =\sqrt[5]{\frac{K_{s p}}{108}} \\ & =\sqrt[5]{\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-72}}{108}}=1.7 \times 10^{-15} \\ \mathrm{Ag}_2 \mathrm{~S} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{K_{s p}}{4}}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-49}}{4}} \\ & =3.4 \times 10^{-17} \\ \mathrm{PbS} & =\sqrt{K_{s p}}=\sqrt{1.1 \times 10^{-29}} \\ & =3.3 \times 10^{-15} \\ \mathrm{CoS} & =\sqrt{K_{s p}}=\sqrt{2 \times 10^{-27}}=4.5 \times 10^{-14}\end{aligned}$
Hence, $\mathrm{Ag}_2 \mathrm{~S}$ is least soluble.
So minimum solubility is of $\mathrm{Ag}_2 \mathrm{~S}$ as its force of attraction is greatest.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $\mathrm{NaOH}(a q), \mathrm{HCl}(a q),$ and $\mathrm{NaCl}(a q)$ concentration of each is $10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$. Their pH will be respectively
questions.solution:
Given $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ion conc. is $10^{-3} \mathrm{M}$ 
we know $\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=10^{-14}\begin{array}{cc}\text { or } & {\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=\frac{10^{-14}}{10^{-3}}} \\ \text { or } & {\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=10^{-11}} \\ \because & \mathrm{pH}=-\log \left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]=-\log \left[10^{-11}\right]\end{array}$
Similarly pH of HCl is 3 and pH of NaCl is 7.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The $K a$ of an acid is $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$. The degree of dissociation of the acid at concentration of 0.2 M is
questions.solution:
From Ostwald's dilution law
$\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{K a}{c}}\begin{aligned} & =\sqrt{\frac{3.2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.2}} \\ & =1.26 \times 10^{-2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The pH of $10^{-8} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaOH}$ is
questions.solution:
For $10^{-8} \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NaOH}$,
$\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=10^{-8}+10^{-7} \quad$ (from water)
$=11 \times 10^{-8}\therefore \quad \mathrm{pOH}=-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=-\log (11 \times 10^{-8})=8-1.04=6.96\therefore \quad \mathrm{pH}=14-6.96=7.04$
